chiliburger-with-or-without-cheese-on-bu.title: Chiliburger (with or without cheese) on bun

content.title: About
content.content: The Chiliburger is a spicy beef patty seasoned with chili, served on a soft bun. The cheese version adds melted cheese (usually cheddar), while the plain version contains only the meat and sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The heat level can be adjusted by changing the type and amount of chili peppers.
It is often topped with pickles, onions, and lettuce to balance the spiciness.
Many restaurants make a house sauce from mayo, tomato, and chili paste.
The bun is lightly toasted to prevent it from becoming soggy from the sauce.
The dish is popular in fast‑food chains and street stalls worldwide.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron, which supports healthy hemoglobin levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The patty supplies B12, B6, and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Capsaicin in chili
items.content: Capsaicin may boost metabolism and has a mild thermogenic effect.

items.title: Calcium from cheese (when added)
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium needed for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: The burger can be calorie‑dense, especially with cheese and sauce, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Spiciness of chili
items.content: Very hot peppers may irritate the stomach of people with sensitive digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Sauces and cheese often contain a lot of salt, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The Chiliburger is best eaten with your hands, holding the bottom of the bun. It pairs well with fries, ranch dressing, or fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burger in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep the bun in a dry place and the meat in an airtight container to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy, nougat filled are sweets consisting of a soft nougat center coated with a chocolate glaze. Nougat is typically made from sugar, honey, egg whites and nuts (often almonds or hazelnuts), giving it a delicate, slightly chewy texture. These candies are popular worldwide and are often given as gifts or enjoyed during celebrations.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nougat originated in the Mediterranean region during antiquity and was used as an energy snack for travelers.
In the United States these treats are often called “chocolate bars,” although they differ from typical bars because the interior is nougat rather than caramel or nuts.
In countries such as Italy, nougat is a traditional Christmas confection.
There are many nougat variations: with nuts, nut‑free, with dried fruit, or flavored with vanilla or coffee.
Nougat production requires precise temperature control; too hot and it becomes hard, too cool and it stays overly soft.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar and honey in the nougat provide quick glucose, which can be useful for low energy levels.

items.title: Contains nuts
items.content: When nuts are included, they add healthy monounsaturated fats, vitamin E and minerals.

items.title: Chocolate antioxidants
items.content: The chocolate coating is rich in flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: These candies may contain almonds, hazelnuts or other nuts that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to tooth decay and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chocolate candy with nougat is fairly calorie‑dense, so it should be enjoyed in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The candies are typically eaten as a dessert or snack. They pair well with coffee, tea or milk. For young children, cut larger pieces into bite‑size portions to reduce choking risk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the candies in a cool, dry place in an airtight container to prevent chocolate melt. At temperatures above 25 °C the chocolate may soften and the nougat become sticky.

content.title: About
content.content: The club sandwich on white bread is a classic multi‑layered sandwich made with toasted white bread, chicken breast, ham, bacon, lettuce, tomato and mayonnaise. It is a staple in cafés and restaurants worldwide and is usually served cut into triangles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first club sandwich appeared in the early 1920s at New York’s Buck’s Club.
Traditionally it consists of three slices of bread and four fillings, creating the characteristic “tower” look.
The original recipe used only turkey, but most modern versions add chicken and ham.
The sandwich is often held together with a toothpick for stability.
In the United States the club sandwich is considered comfort food and frequently appears on brunch menus.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken, ham and bacon provide a high amount of protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat components contain niacin, vitamin B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains vegetables
items.content: Tomato and lettuce add vitamin C, potassium and antioxidants.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The sandwich delivers a fast supply of calories, making it a satisfying snack.

items.title: Calcium from cheese (optional)
items.content: Adding a slice of cheese increases calcium content, beneficial for bones.

items.title: High in fat and sodium
items.content: Bacon and ham can be high in saturated fat and salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Egg and dairy allergy
items.content: Mayonnaise is typically made with eggs and oil, posing a risk for allergic individuals.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked bacon or chicken can harbor salmonella or campylobacter.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: A three‑layer club easily exceeds 600 kcal, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is usually served cut into three triangles and held together with a toothpick. It can be eaten with the hands, though a knife and fork are also acceptable.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Club sandwiches are best eaten immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator wrapped in plastic wrap for no more than 24 hours. Bread may become soggy and mayonnaise may separate.

collards-frozen-cooked-fat-added-ns-as-t.title: Collards, frozen, cooked, fat added, NS (fat type 4341)

content.title: About
content.content: Collards are leafy vegetables from the Brassica family. This product is flash‑frozen after cooking and has added vegetable fat to enhance flavor and texture. It is ready to eat after reheating.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Collards are rich in vitamins K, A and C.
They are a staple in Southern U.S. cuisine, often featured in "soul food" dishes.
Freezing shortly after cooking preserves most nutrients.
Added fat improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Collards are commonly used in stews, soups, and as a side dish.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K supports blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fiber promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Vitamins A and C help combat free radicals.

items.title: Improved nutrient absorption
items.content: The added vegetable fat aids the uptake of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: When consumed in moderation, it fits well into calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Allergy to added fats
items.content: Some individuals may react to the vegetable oil used.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The product may contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Texture loss if overheated
items.content: Overcooking can make the leaves soggy and watery.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reheat the product in a skillet or microwave until hot. Serve as a side to meat, fish, or incorporate into vegetable stews. Add seasonings, garlic, or a squeeze of lemon to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C or lower. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and store in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Potato, scalloped, ready-to-heat is a single‑serve, fully cooked dish consisting of thinly sliced potatoes baked in a creamy cheese sauce with herbs and spices. The package is designed for quick preparation in a microwave or conventional oven.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic "scalloped potatoes" dish originated in English‑speaking cuisine in the 19th century.
Starchy varieties such as Russet are preferred for their fluffy texture when baked.
The sauce is typically made from milk, cream, and grated Cheddar cheese.
The frozen product can be stored for up to 12 months without loss of quality.
Microwave heating usually takes 3‑5 minutes, while oven heating requires 15‑20 minutes.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Offers slowly digestible carbs that help maintain satiety.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce adds calcium needed for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike many convenience meals, this product contains no added sugars.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The creamy sauce and cheese make the dish relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Contains dairy
items.content: Milk and cheese may trigger allergies or lactose intolerance in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Added salt increases sodium intake, which should be limited by people with hypertension.

items.title: Requires thorough heating
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave cold spots, increasing the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the package in a microwave (800 W for about 4‑5 minutes) or in an oven at 180 °C for 15‑20 minutes until piping hot. Serve as a side dish with meat or fish, or enjoy it on its own, garnished with fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, cook immediately and do not keep at room temperature for more than 2 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) is an evergreen aromatic shrub in the mint family, native to the Mediterranean. It has tough needle-like leaves with a pine-like, camphor-spicy aroma and a slightly bitter flavor. Rosemary is used fresh and dried for meat, potatoes, bread, marinades, oils, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name rosemary comes from Latin words meaning sea dew.
In 2017, botanists moved rosemary into the sage genus and began calling it Salvia rosmarinus.
In ancient times, rosemary was considered a symbol of remembrance and fidelity.
It pairs excellently with grilled meat, potatoes, and bread, such as focaccia.
Tough rosemary sprigs can be used in place of skewers.

items.title: Contains rosmarinic and carnosic acids
items.content: These compounds have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains essential oils
items.content: Aromatic compounds give rosemary its characteristic smell.

items.title: Adds flavor without calories or salt
items.content: Fragrant herbs make dishes more flavorful without extra salt or fat.

items.title: May reduce harmful compounds when grilling
items.content: A marinade with rosemary may reduce the formation of harmful compounds when grilling meat.

items.title: Contains a small amount of minerals
items.content: The herb contains calcium, iron, and manganese, but the amounts in a dish are small.

items.title: Large amounts and pregnancy
items.content: Rosemary is safe in food amounts, but large amounts and concentrated supplements during pregnancy should be discussed with a doctor.

items.title: Epilepsy and essential oil
items.content: Rosemary essential oil contains camphor and may trigger seizures; it should not be taken internally, and people with epilepsy should be careful.

items.title: Medications
items.content: In large amounts, rosemary may affect how anticoagulants and some other medications work.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions and contact dermatitis are possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Finely chop the rosemary needles and add them to meat, chicken, fish, potatoes, vegetables, bread, soups, marinades, and oils. Fresh sprigs can be put whole into a dish and removed before serving. Less dried rosemary is needed than fresh.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh sprigs in the refrigerator, wrapped in a damp paper towel, for one to two weeks, or freeze or dry them. Keep dried rosemary in an airtight jar in a dry, dark place.
